result.markdown: --- title: "One model, many switches" subtitle: "Measuring the effect of biological realism like for like" engine: julia --- ## Why a second vignette The [first vignette](../01_building_realism/01_building_realism.md) built up realism along a ladder in three host–pathogen systems. Those systems start from three different published models, so their steps cannot be compared directly, and a ladder adds things in one order only. This vignette uses a single **nested model** in which each piece of biology is a switch. With every switch off it is the simplest possible model: susceptible and infectious adults. Any combination of switches can be turned on, so that: - every model is compared with every other like for like; - the effect of one piece of realism can be measured against every setting of the others; - the same comparison can be repeated in different conditions. | Switch | What it adds | |---|---| | `latent` | infected animals are not infectious at once | | `environment` | half of transmission goes through a pool of zoospores that outlasts the animals that shed them (total transmission unchanged) | | `load` | infections start light (little shedding, no disease death) and progress to heavy | | `recovery` | infected animals can clear the infection (with `load` on, only light infections) | | `larvae` | an aquatic larval stage between birth and adulthood | | `larval_infection` | larvae are infected by adults (and from the pool when `environment` is on), without disease, and half carry the infection through metamorphosis | ::: {.callout-important} The model is anchored on the Bsal model of Schmidt et al. (2017) for fire salamanders: with only `latent` on it is their published model, with their parameter values. The carry-over through metamorphosis is from Wang et al. (2021), read from the package's compendium. **Everything else is new work in this package and is not a published result**, and the values attached to the other switches (pool half-life 30 days, light infections shedding 10% as much and lasting about two weeks (one week when they can also recover), recovery at the same rate as progression, a four-month larval stage) are illustrative. ::: ## The model ### State Each animal is an adult or a larva, untreated (u) or treated (t), and in one infection class. Adults are susceptible ($S$), latent ($L$), lightly infected ($Y$) or heavily infected ($I$). Larvae are uninfected ($S^w$) or infected ($I^w$). With the zoospore pool $Z$ this gives 17 variables. Densities are per hectare and time is in years. A class whose switch is off stays empty. ### The simplest model With every switch off and no treatment, there are only susceptible and infectious adults: $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{dS}{dt} &= bS - \beta I S - (d + \gamma N) S, \\ \frac{dI}{dt} &= \beta I S - d_I I - (d + \gamma N) I, \end{aligned} $$ with $N = S + I$ and $\gamma = (b - d)/K$, so that the population without Bsal settles at $K$. Only susceptible adults reproduce. Turning on `latent` puts the class $L$ between $S$ and $I$, left at rate $e$; this is equation 2.1 of Schmidt et al. (2017). ### The full model ::: {#4 .cell execution_count=1} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ![The nested model with every switch on, for untreated animals. Blue boxes and arrows belong to the switch named in brackets; the dotted arrow is used instead of the larval stage when `larvae` is off. Dashed grey arrows are influences, not flows: shedding H by light and heavy adults feeds the infectious pressure Q directly and, with `environment` on, through the zoospore pool Z. Natural deaths (rate D for adults, μw for larvae) leave every box and are not drawn.](02_nested_model_files/figure-html/cell-3-output-1.svg){} ::: ::: Adults shed zoospores, light infections a fraction $\rho$ as much as heavy ones. Adults are infected at rate $\beta Q$ per susceptible animal, larvae at $\beta_w Q$, where $$ \begin{aligned} H &= \sum_{\tau} h_\tau \left( \rho Y_\tau + I_\tau \right), \\ Q &= (1 - \phi) H + \phi \mu_Z Z, \\ \frac{dZ}{dt} &= H - \mu_Z Z. \end{aligned} $$ At equilibrium $\mu_Z Z = H$, so the pool changes the timing of transmission but not its total. Larvae do not shed. For adults with treatment label $\tau \in \{\mathrm{u}, \mathrm{t}\}$: $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{dS_\tau}{dt} &= B^A_\tau + M^S_\tau - f_\tau \beta Q S_\tau + \sigma Y_\tau - D S_\tau + \Omega(S_\tau), \\ \frac{dL_\tau}{dt} &= f_\tau \beta Q S_\tau + M^I_\tau - e L_\tau - D L_\tau + \Omega(L_\tau), \\ \frac{dY_\tau}{dt} &= e L_\tau - (\nu + \sigma) Y_\tau - D Y_\tau + \Omega(Y_\tau), \\ \frac{dI_\tau}{dt} &= \nu Y_\tau - k_\tau d_I I_\tau - D I_\tau + \Omega(I_\tau), \end{aligned} $$ where $D = d + \gamma N_A$ and $N_A$ is the density of all adults. Density dependence acts on adults only. For larvae: $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{dS^w_\tau}{dt} &= B^w_\tau - f_\tau \beta_w Q S^w_\tau - (m + \mu_w) S^w_\tau + \Omega(S^w_\tau), \\ \frac{dI^w_\tau}{dt} &= f_\tau \beta_w Q S^w_\tau - (m + \mu_w) I^w_\tau + \Omega(I^w_\tau). \end{aligned} $$ Births are $$ B = b' \sum_{\tau} \left[ S_\tau + Y_\tau + (1 - k_\tau)(L_\tau + I_\tau) \right], $$ and all are untreated: $B^w_{\mathrm{u}} = B$ with larvae, $B^A_{\mathrm{u}} = B$ without, and the other birth terms are zero. Without larvae $b' = b$; with them $b' = b (m + \mu_w)/m$, so that each adult still recruits $b$ adults a year when there is no Bsal. Untreated latent and heavily infected adults do not reproduce, as in Schmidt et al. (2017). Light infections do. Treated latent and heavily infected adults reproduce in proportion to the treatment's tolerance. At metamorphosis (rate $m$) an infected larva stays infected with probability $p$ and enters the latent class; otherwise it becomes a susceptible adult. Untreated larvae become untreated adults. A fraction $r$ (`retention`) of treated larvae keep the treatment and the rest lose it: $$ \begin{aligned} M^S_{\mathrm{u}} &= m \left[ S^w_{\mathrm{u}} + (1 - p) I^w_{\mathrm{u}} \right] + (1 - r)\, m \left[ S^w_{\mathrm{t}} + (1 - p) I^w_{\mathrm{t}} \right], \\ M^S_{\mathrm{t}} &= r\, m \left[ S^w_{\mathrm{t}} + (1 - p) I^w_{\mathrm{t}} \right], \\ M^I_{\mathrm{u}} &= p\, m \left[ I^w_{\mathrm{u}} + (1 - r) I^w_{\mathrm{t}} \right], \\ M^I_{\mathrm{t}} &= r\, p\, m\, I^w_{\mathrm{t}}. \end{aligned} $$ #### Switching pieces off Each switch removes terms; nothing else changes. - `latent` off: $L$ is skipped. New infections, and infected larvae at metamorphosis, enter $Y$ (or $I$ if `load` is also off). - `load` off: $Y$ is skipped. Latent animals, or new infections, go straight to $I$, and recovery is from $I$ to $S$ at rate $\sigma$. Shedding is $H = \sum_\tau h_\tau I_\tau$. With `load` on, only light infections recover. - `recovery` off: $\sigma = 0$. - `environment` off: $\phi = 0$, so $Q = H$ and $Z$ plays no part. - `larvae` off: there are no larval classes and no $M$ terms; births enter $S_{\mathrm{u}}$ and $b' = b$. - `larval_infection` off: $\beta_w = 0$, so larvae stay uninfected. Latent animals and infected larvae never recover, and infected larvae do not die of the disease. ### Treatment Treatment scales three rates. Each effect is multiplied by the protection $g$ that remains: $$ f_{\mathrm{u}} = h_{\mathrm{u}} = k_{\mathrm{u}} = 1, \qquad f_{\mathrm{t}} = 1 - g\varepsilon, \qquad h_{\mathrm{t}} = 1 - g\zeta, \qquad k_{\mathrm{t}} = 1 - g\theta. $$ Efficacy $\varepsilon$ cuts the infection rate, tolerance $\theta$ cuts disease deaths (the animal stays infectious) and $\zeta$ cuts shedding. The **block** treatment of this vignette is $\varepsilon = 0.99$; the **survive** treatment is $\theta = 0.99$. Protection can wane with the abundance of the applied bacteria, $$ g(a) = \frac{1 + 1/\kappa}{1 + 2^{a / t_B} / \kappa}, $$ where $a$ is the time since the last application, $t_B$ the bacteria's half-life and $\kappa$ their starting abundance over the abundance that gives half the effect. Without waning, as here, $g = 1$. Animals also gain and lose the bacteria. For any class $X$ in stage $s$, $$ \Omega(X_{\mathrm{u}}) = -\delta F_s X_{\mathrm{u}} + \omega X_{\mathrm{t}}, \qquad \Omega(X_{\mathrm{t}}) = \delta F_s X_{\mathrm{u}} - \omega X_{\mathrm{t}}, $$ where $F_s$ is the treated fraction of that stage, $\delta$ the rate of spread and $\omega = \ln 2 / (\text{half-life})$ the rate of loss. Both are zero in this vignette. At each treatment time a fraction $c$ (`coverage`) of the untreated animals of the treated stage becomes treated, and the clock $a$ restarts. ::: {#6 .cell execution_count=1} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ![The treatment layer. Every infection class X of the diagram above has an untreated (grey) and a treated (blue) copy. Treated animals gain and lose the bacteria within a stage; at metamorphosis a fraction r of treated larvae stay treated. In this vignette δ = ω = r = 0 and g = 1.](02_nested_model_files/figure-html/cell-4-output-1.svg){} ::: ::: ### Arrival and fade-out The population starts without Bsal: $S_{\mathrm{u}} = K$ and, with larvae, $S^w_{\mathrm{u}} = bK/m$. Bsal arrives as $I_0 = 0.01$ heavily infected untreated adults per hectare (one per km², as in Schmidt et al. 2017), after any treatment at the same time. The fade-out rule, when used, is checked after every solver step with threshold $n_{\min}$ (`fadeout_density`): if all animals together fall below $n_{\min}$ they are set to zero; otherwise, once Bsal has arrived, if $0 < \sum (\text{infected animals}) + \mu_Z Z < n_{\min}$, every infected class and the pool are set to zero. The infected animals are removed, not returned to the susceptible class. The growth rate reported below is the largest real part of the eigenvalues of the Jacobian of the infected classes ($L$, $Y$, $I$, $I^w$ and $Z$, untreated) at this disease-free state. ### Symbols | Symbol | Meaning | Value or source | |---|---|---| | $b$ | recruitment, per adult | 0.39 per yr, compendium (schmidt2017) | | $d$ | natural death | 0.125 per yr, compendium (schmidt2017) | | $d_I$ | Bsal death of heavy infections | 52 per yr, compendium (schmidt2017) | | $e$ | latent to infectious | 364 per yr, compendium (schmidt2017) | | $\beta$ | transmission to adults | 52 ha per yr, compendium (schmidt2017) | | $K$ | carrying capacity | 25 per ha, compendium (schmidt2017); also 3 and 1.5 below | | $\gamma$ | density dependence | $(b - d)/K$ | | $\phi$ | share of transmission through the pool | 0.5, illustrative | | $\mu_Z$ | pool decay | $\ln 2$ / 30 days, illustrative | | $\rho$ | shedding of a light infection relative to a heavy one | 0.1, illustrative | | $\nu$ | light to heavy | 26 per yr, illustrative | | $\sigma$ | recovery | 26 per yr, illustrative | | $m$ | metamorphosis, 1/(larval period) | 1/(0.33 yr), illustrative | | $\mu_w$ | larval death | 1 per yr, illustrative | | $\beta_w$ | transmission from adults to larvae | 5.2 ha per yr, illustrative | | $p$ | infected larvae still infected after metamorphosis | 0.5 (5 of 10), compendium (wang2021) | | $\varepsilon$, $\theta$, $\zeta$ | treatment efficacy, tolerance, shedding reduction | 0.99 (block), 0.99 (survive), 0; illustrative | | $g$, $\kappa$, $t_B$ | remaining protection and its waning | $g = 1$ (no waning) | | $\delta$, $\omega$ | spread and loss of the bacteria | 0 | | $c$, $r$ | coverage, retention at metamorphosis | $c = 1$ when treated, $r = 0$ | | $I_0$ | arriving infected adults | 0.01 per ha | | $n_{\min}$ | fade-out threshold | $10^{-4}$ per ha, illustrative | ::: {#8 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using Chytridiomycosis, Plots, Printf default(linewidth = 2, size = (720, 380), legendfontsize = 8, guidefontsize = 9, titlefontsize = 10, left_margin = 4Plots.mm, bottom_margin = 4Plots.mm) T(; kw...) = MicrobiomeTreatment(; kw...) bio(; kw...) = ChytridBiology(:wang2021; kw...) schmidt = SchmidtParameters(:schmidt2017) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` SchmidtParameters{Float64}(0.39, 0.125, 52.0, 364.0, 52.0, 25.0, 0.0625, 1.0) ``` ::: ::: ## The outcomes Bsal arrives in a population at carrying capacity. Four things are recorded for each model: - the pathogen's initial **growth rate**; - **untreated**: mean adults over the next ten years, as a fraction of carrying capacity; - **block**: the same, with every adult treated once with bacteria that block 99% of infections for life; - **survive**: the same, with bacteria that prevent 99% of disease deaths and do not block infection. This is the kind of protection seen in trials. ::: {#10 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function outcomes(p, b) run(tr; kw...) = solve(NestedChytridProblem(p, b, tr; kw...)) u = run(T()) bl, sv = run(T(efficacy = 0.99); coverage = 1.0), run(T(tolerance = 0.99); coverage = 1.0) fate(r) = !isnan(r.host_extinction) ? :host_lost : !isnan(r.pathogen_fadeout) ? :pathogen_gone : :both_persist return (growth = invasion_growth_rate(p, b), untreated = u.mean_adults, lowest = u.min_adults, block = bl.mean_adults, survive = sv.mean_adults, fates = (fate(u), fate(bl), fate(sv))) end ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` outcomes (generic function with 1 method) ``` ::: ::: A check first: with only the latent class switched on, the growth rate equals the one that follows from the equations of Schmidt et al. (2017). ::: {#12 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} p = schmidt λ = (sqrt((p.e - p.d_I)^2 + 4 * p.e * p.β * p.K) - 2p.b - p.d_I - p.e) / 2 (nested = invasion_growth_rate(p, bio(latent = true)), schmidt = λ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (nested = 496.972318234428, schmidt = 496.97231824502785) ``` ::: ::: ## A ladder in one model The switches are turned on one after another, starting from the simplest model. ::: {#14 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} order = [:latent, :environment, :load, :recovery, :larvae, :larval_infection] names_ = ["simplest: S and I", "+ latent period", "+ environmental pool", "+ light and heavy infections", "+ recovery", "+ larval stage", "+ larvae infected"] ladder_models(p) = [outcomes(p, bio(; (k => true for k in order[1:i])...)) for i in 0:length(order)] function ladder_figure(rows, title) k = length(rows) bar((1:k) .- 0.27, [r.untreated for r in rows]; orientation = :h, bar_width = 0.25, label = "no treatment", color = :gray70, yticks = (1:k, names_), yflip = true, xlims = (0, 1.05), xticks = 0:0.25:1, xlabel = "mean adults over 10 years, fraction of K", size = (840, 80 + 44k), left_margin = 6Plots.mm, legend = :outertop, legend_column = 3, title) bar!(1:k, [r.block for r in rows]; orientation = :h, bar_width = 0.25, label = "block infection", color = :steelblue) bar!((1:k) .+ 0.27, [r.survive for r in rows]; orientation = :h, bar_width = 0.25, label = "survive infection", color = :darkorange) end function ladder_table(rows) println("| Model | Growth rate (per yr) | Untreated | Lowest untreated | Block | Survive |") println("|---|---|---|---|---|---|") for (n, r) in zip(names_, rows) @printf("| %s | %.0f | %.3f | %.0e | %.3f | %.3f |\n", n, r.growth, r.untreated, r.lowest, r.block, r.survive) end end high = ladder_models(schmidt) ladder_figure(high, "Schmidt's density: 25 per ha, R0 = 24.8") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ``` {.julia .cell-code} ladder_table(high) ``` | Model | Growth rate (per yr) | Untreated | Lowest untreated | Block | Survive | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | simplest: S and I | 1248 | 0.003 | 2e-11 | 0.338 | 0.132 | | + latent period | 497 | 0.004 | 2e-11 | 0.338 | 0.132 | | + environmental pool | 309 | 0.005 | 2e-11 | 0.339 | 0.133 | | + light and heavy infections | 111 | 0.012 | 6e-06 | 0.331 | 0.138 | | + recovery | 98 | 0.023 | 2e-03 | 0.382 | 0.139 | | + larval stage | 98 | 0.074 | 2e-02 | 0.380 | 0.140 | | + larvae infected | 98 | 0.073 | 2e-02 | 0.379 | 0.140 | At the density Schmidt et al. used, where Bsal's reproduction number is about 25, **the added biology changes the conclusions very little**. The epidemic slows more than ten-fold as switches are turned on, but the population collapses in every model, and each treatment gives almost the same result throughout. One thing does change: the lowest density the untreated population reaches rises by many orders of magnitude, which matters for whether it could go extinct. ## Every combination A ladder is one path. The four switches for the adult stage are now set in every combination, with three settings for the larvae (none, present but not infected, infected): 48 models. ::: {#18 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} configs = vec([(; latent, environment, load, recovery, larvae = lv > 0, larval_infection = lv > 1) for latent in (false, true), environment in (false, true), load in (false, true), recovery in (false, true), lv in 0:2]) all_models(p; fade = 0.0) = [(c, outcomes(p, bio(; fadeout_density = fade, c...))) for c in configs] same(c, c2, skip) = all(getfield(c, k) == getfield(c2, k) for k in keys(c) if !(k in skip)) pieces = [ ("latent period", c -> c.latent, (c, c2) -> !c2.latent && same(c, c2, (:latent,))), ("environmental pool", c -> c.environment, (c, c2) -> !c2.environment && same(c, c2, (:environment,))), ("light and heavy infections", c -> c.load, (c, c2) -> !c2.load && same(c, c2, (:load,))), ("recovery", c -> c.recovery, (c, c2) -> !c2.recovery && same(c, c2, (:recovery,))), ("larval stage", c -> c.larvae && !c.larval_infection, (c, c2) -> !c2.larvae && same(c, c2, (:larvae, :larval_infection))), ("larvae infected", c -> c.larval_infection, (c, c2) -> c2.larvae && !c2.larval_infection && same(c, c2, (:larvae, :larval_infection))), ] # change in an outcome when a piece is switched on, for every setting of the other pieces effects(res, on, off, f) = [f(o) - f(o2) for (c, o) in res if on(c) for (c2, o2) in res if off(c, c2)] function effects_table(res) println("| Piece switched on | Untreated: mean (range) | Block: mean (range) | Survive: mean (range) |") println("|---|---|---|---|") for (label, on, off) in pieces cells = map((o -> o.untreated, o -> o.block, o -> o.survive)) do f d = effects(res, on, off, f) @sprintf("%+.2f (%+.2f to %+.2f)", sum(d) / length(d), minimum(d), maximum(d)) end println("| ", label, " | ", join(cells, " | "), " |") end end function spread_figure(res, title) f = (o -> o.untreated, o -> o.block, o -> o.survive) labels = ["no treatment", "block infection", "survive infection"] plot(; xticks = (1:3, labels), xlims = (0.5, 3.5), ylims = (0, 1.05), ylabel = "mean adults, fraction of K", legend = false, title, size = (640, 360)) for (i, g) in enumerate(f) v = [g(o) for (_, o) in res] scatter!(i .+ range(-0.18, 0.18; length = length(v)), sort(v); markersize = 4, color = (:gray50, :steelblue, :darkorange)[i], markerstrokewidth = 0) end current() end res_high = all_models(schmidt) spread_figure(res_high, "48 models at 25 per ha (R0 = 24.8)") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ``` {.julia .cell-code} effects_table(res_high) ``` | Piece switched on | Untreated: mean (range) | Block: mean (range) | Survive: mean (range) | |---|---|---|---| | latent period | +0.00 (+0.00 to +0.00) | +0.00 (+0.00 to +0.00) | +0.00 (+0.00 to +0.01) | | environmental pool | -0.02 (-0.08 to +0.00) | +0.00 (+0.00 to +0.00) | +0.00 (-0.00 to +0.00) | | light and heavy infections | +0.01 (-0.00 to +0.02) | +0.00 (-0.01 to +0.01) | -0.00 (-0.01 to +0.01) | | recovery | +0.03 (+0.00 to +0.09) | +0.04 (+0.03 to +0.05) | +0.01 (+0.00 to +0.02) | | larval stage | +0.02 (-0.03 to +0.05) | -0.00 (-0.00 to -0.00) | +0.00 (+0.00 to +0.00) | | larvae infected | -0.00 (-0.01 to -0.00) | -0.00 (-0.00 to -0.00) | -0.00 (-0.00 to -0.00) | Each dot is one of the 48 models. At this density they sit almost on top of each other: no piece of host biology moves any outcome by more than about 0.1. When the pathogen spreads this fast and kills this quickly, the simple model gives the same answer as the complex one. ## The same comparison nearer the threshold Schmidt et al. show that Bsal cannot invade below about one adult female per hectare. The comparison is repeated at 3 per hectare (reproduction number 3) and 1.5 per hectare (1.5). ::: {#22 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} mid, low = Chytridiomycosis.with(schmidt; K = 3.0), Chytridiomycosis.with(schmidt; K = 1.5) res_mid, res_low = all_models(mid), all_models(low) spread_figure(res_mid, "48 models at 3 per ha (R0 = 3.0)") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ``` {.julia .cell-code} effects_table(res_mid) ``` | Piece switched on | Untreated: mean (range) | Block: mean (range) | Survive: mean (range) | |---|---|---|---| | latent period | +0.01 (-0.00 to +0.09) | +0.03 (-0.00 to +0.39) | +0.00 (+0.00 to +0.00) | | environmental pool | -0.02 (-0.09 to +0.03) | -0.10 (-0.39 to +0.01) | -0.00 (-0.03 to +0.00) | | light and heavy infections | +0.01 (-0.07 to +0.09) | -0.03 (-0.42 to +0.06) | -0.09 (-0.20 to +0.01) | | recovery | +0.30 (+0.17 to +0.47) | +0.22 (+0.00 to +0.42) | +0.10 (+0.01 to +0.21) | | larval stage | +0.04 (-0.06 to +0.13) | +0.00 (-0.00 to +0.00) | -0.00 (-0.01 to +0.00) | | larvae infected | -0.03 (-0.11 to -0.00) | -0.09 (-0.40 to -0.00) | -0.00 (-0.00 to -0.00) | ::: {#26 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} spread_figure(res_low, "48 models at 1.5 per ha (R0 = 1.5)") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ``` {.julia .cell-code} effects_table(res_low) ``` | Piece switched on | Untreated: mean (range) | Block: mean (range) | Survive: mean (range) | |---|---|---|---| | latent period | +0.00 (+0.00 to +0.05) | +0.00 (-0.00 to +0.00) | +0.00 (-0.00 to +0.00) | | environmental pool | -0.00 (-0.04 to +0.03) | -0.05 (-0.19 to +0.02) | -0.01 (-0.05 to +0.01) | | light and heavy infections | -0.04 (-0.12 to +0.02) | -0.02 (-0.08 to -0.00) | -0.18 (-0.41 to +0.01) | | recovery | +0.36 (+0.26 to +0.43) | +0.11 (+0.00 to +0.20) | +0.21 (+0.01 to +0.43) | | larval stage | -0.00 (-0.04 to +0.01) | +0.00 (-0.00 to +0.00) | -0.00 (-0.01 to +0.00) | | larvae infected | -0.01 (-0.07 to -0.00) | -0.04 (-0.19 to -0.00) | -0.00 (-0.00 to -0.00) | Now the models disagree. At 3 per hectare the untreated outcome ranges from 0.15 to 0.62 depending on which biology is included, and the infection-blocking treatment from 0.57 to full protection. **Realism matters most near the threshold.** The ladder at 3 per hectare: ::: {#30 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} ladder_figure(ladder_models(mid), "3 per ha, R0 = 3.0") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: Three things stand out. 1. **Recovery is the piece that matters most**, for the untreated population and for the blocking treatment. This project has no estimate of it for Bsal. 2. **Pieces do not have a fixed effect.** The ranges in the tables are wide: an environmental pool, or infected larvae, changes the blocking treatment by anything from nothing to −0.4 depending on what else is in the model. 3. **Bacteria that let animals survive infection do worse than no treatment** at these densities, in every one of the 48 models (orange below grey; counts in the table below). Untreated, an epidemic at low density burns out and the population recovers. Treated animals that survive stay infectious in this model, and keep infecting the untreated animals born after them. ``` {.julia .cell-code} println("| Density | Models in which the survive treatment does worse than none | Blocking does worse than none |") println("|---|---|---|") for (label, res) in (("25 per ha", res_high), ("3 per ha", res_mid), ("1.5 per ha", res_low)) @printf("| %s | %d of 48 | %d of 48 |\n", label, count(x -> x[2].survive < x[2].untreated, res), count(x -> x[2].block < x[2].untreated - 1e-6, res)) end ``` | Density | Models in which the survive treatment does worse than none | Blocking does worse than none | |---|---|---| | 25 per ha | 0 of 48 | 0 of 48 | | 3 per ha | 48 of 48 | 0 of 48 | | 1.5 per ha | 48 of 48 | 0 of 48 | ## A fade-out rule The equations are deterministic, so a density can fall to a value that means far less than one animal and then grow back. Near the threshold that can decide the result. The model is therefore given a fade-out rule, itself a piece of realism: once infected animals (adults and larvae, with the zoospore pool counted in infectious-animal equivalents) fall below one per 100 km² (0.0001 per hectare) the pathogen is removed, and if all animals fall below that density the host population is removed. The effect of each piece when it is the first thing added to the simplest model, and when it is the last thing added to the otherwise complete model, at 3 per hectare with the fade-out rule: ``` {.julia .cell-code} full = (latent = true, environment = true, load = true, recovery = true, larvae = true, larval_infection = true) empty_ = (latent = false, environment = false, load = false, recovery = false, larvae = false, larval_infection = false) get_(res, c) = only(o for (c2, o) in res if c2 == c) println("| Piece | Untreated: added first | added last | Block: added first | added last |") println("|---|---|---|---|---|") for (label, on, off) in (("latent period", (latent = true,), (latent = false,)), ("environmental pool", (environment = true,), (environment = false,)), ("light and heavy infections", (load = true,), (load = false,)), ("recovery", (recovery = true,), (recovery = false,)), ("larval stage, infected", (larvae = true, larval_infection = true), (larvae = false, larval_infection = false))) first_ = (get_(fres_mid, merge(empty_, on)), get_(fres_mid, empty_)) last_ = (get_(fres_mid, full), get_(fres_mid, merge(full, off))) @printf("| %s | %+.2f | %+.2f | %+.2f | %+.2f |\n", label, first_[1].untreated - first_[2].untreated, last_[1].untreated - last_[2].untreated, first_[1].block - first_[2].block, last_[1].block - last_[2].block) end ``` | Piece | Untreated: added first | added last | Block: added first | added last | |---|---|---|---|---| | latent period | +0.00 | +0.00 | -0.00 | -0.00 | | environmental pool | +0.00 | -0.04 | -0.00 | -0.00 | | light and heavy infections | -0.07 | +0.08 | -0.00 | -0.00 | | recovery | +0.33 | +0.37 | +0.00 | +0.42 | | larval stage, infected | +0.10 | -0.01 | -0.00 | -0.00 | Where the two columns differ, the piece interacts with the others, and a ladder would give a different impression depending on where the piece was placed. ## A stochastic version A fade-out rule is a crude stand-in for chance. The model also exists in a stochastic form, `StochasticNestedProblem`, in which animals are whole numbers in a given area and every transition happens at random. It draws its events from the same list of transitions as the equations, so with a large enough area it reproduces them, and with one infected animal its chance of a major outbreak matches the theoretical $1 - 1/R_0$ (both are checked in the package tests). Bsal now arrives as **one infected adult** in **20 hectares**: 500 adults at Schmidt's density, 60 at 3 per hectare and 30 at 1.5. Each model is run 100 times. The stochastic version counts animals, $n_i = A x_i$ in an area $A$. Time moves in steps of $\Delta t$ = 6 hours. At the start of each step every flow of the equations above is turned into a rate per animal, $\lambda_{ij}$ from class $i$ to destination $j$ (a death is one destination). Then $$ \begin{aligned} O_i &\sim \text{Binomial}\left(n_i,\ 1 - e^{-\Lambda_i \Delta t}\right), \qquad \Lambda_i = \sum_j \lambda_{ij}, \\ (O_{i \to j})_j &\sim \text{Multinomial}\left(O_i,\ (\lambda_{ij} / \Lambda_i)_j\right), \\ \text{births} &\sim \text{Poisson}\left(A B \Delta t\right). \end{aligned} $$ The pool stays continuous and is updated exactly with shedding held at its value at the start of the step: $Z \leftarrow Z e^{-\mu_Z \Delta t} + (H/\mu_Z)(1 - e^{-\mu_Z \Delta t})$. At a treatment each untreated animal is treated with probability $c$. The fade-out rule is not used. Bsal is lost when no animal is infected and the pool is expected to cause fewer than 0.05 more infections ($\beta \phi Z S < 0.05$, with $S$ the number of susceptible animals); the pool is then emptied. ::: {#44 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using Random: Xoshiro reps, area = 100, 20.0 function stochastic_fates(p, b, tr, cov; area = area) runs = [solve(StochasticNestedProblem(p, b, tr; area, coverage = cov); rng = Xoshiro(s)) for s in 1:reps] host = count(r -> !isnan(r.host_extinction), runs) / reps gone = count(r -> isnan(r.host_extinction) && !isnan(r.pathogen_extinction), runs) / reps return (host = host, gone = gone, both = 1 - host - gone, minor = count(r -> r.peak_infected < 10, runs) / reps, mean = sum(r.mean_adults for r in runs) / reps) end ladder_bios = [bio(; (k => true for k in order[1:i])...) for i in 0:length(order)] treatments = (("no treatment", T(), 0.0), ("block infection", T(efficacy = 0.99), 1.0), ("survive infection", T(tolerance = 0.99), 1.0)) densities = (("25 per ha", schmidt), ("3 per ha", mid), ("1.5 per ha", low)) sto = Dict((d, t, i) => stochastic_fates(p, b, tr, cov) for (d, p) in densities for (t, tr, cov) in treatments for (i, b) in enumerate(ladder_bios)) nothing ``` ::: ### One run against the equations At Schmidt's density, with every adult treated on arrival with bacteria that block 99% of infections, the equations give about a third of the population after ten years (step 1 of the ladder above). Ten stochastic runs of the same model: ::: {#46 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} b1 = bio(latent = true) det = solve(NestedChytridProblem(schmidt, b1, T(efficacy = 0.99); coverage = 1.0)) plt = plot(det.t, det.adults ./ schmidt.K; color = :black, linewidth = 3, label = "equations", xlabel = "years since Bsal arrived", ylabel = "adults (fraction of K)", ylims = (0, 1.15), legend = :bottomleft) for s in 1:10 r = solve(StochasticNestedProblem(schmidt, b1, T(efficacy = 0.99); area, coverage = 1.0); rng = Xoshiro(s)) plot!(plt, r.t, r.adults ./ r.adults[1]; color = :steelblue, alpha = 0.6, linewidth = 1, label = s == 1 ? kept), against a third in the equations. Pieces of biology that make a chain of infection last longer (an environmental pool, light infections, infected larvae) bring it down to between 0.73 and 0.83, because they give untreated young time to be born before Bsal is gone. 2. **Without treatment, the simple models lose the host.** At Schmidt's density the host population disappears in almost every run of the four simplest models. With recovery it survives in about half, and with a larval stage in all. The larval refuge seen in the equations is real, not an artefact. 3. **Near the threshold most introductions fizzle.** At 1.5 per hectare most single introductions never become an outbreak, and with recovery or larvae nearly all of them. 4. **The survive-type treatment often loses the host in small populations.** In 20 hectares it loses the host in about 30 to 60% of runs at every density. Near the threshold, and in every model with a larval stage, that is more often than with no treatment at all. ### Does the size of the population matter? In 20 hectares, the treated animals that survive and keep Bsal going are too few to outlast the untreated young it kills. ## What this shows 1. **Whether realism matters depends on the regime.** For a pathogen far above its invasion threshold, six pieces of host biology barely change the outcome or the value of treatment. Near the threshold the same pieces change both a great deal. 2. **So the first question is where the system sits.** Far above the threshold, the deterministic models agree with each other. In sparser populations the answer depends on biology that has not been measured, recovery above all. 3. **Effects of single pieces are not transferable.** They vary with the rest of the model, so the result of adding one piece to a simple model should not be read as the effect of that piece. 4. **Protection that keeps infected animals alive can be worse than none**, where the untreated epidemic would have burnt out. 5. **A model can mislead through its mathematics as well as its biology.** One apparent effect disappeared under a fade-out rule. More importantly, the deterministic models all agreed that blocking infection in every adult on arrival leaves about a third of a dense population, and the stochastic version shows that result was made of fractions of an animal: with whole animals, Bsal nearly always dies out first. 6. **Chance is a piece of realism like the others, and here it was the largest.** Agreement among the 48 deterministic models at Schmidt's density did not mean the answer was robust: all of them shared the same mathematical assumption. ## Limits - The nested model covers the salamander system only. The toad and frog systems of the first vignette have features it lacks: a seasonal cohort, and a continuous load on each animal. - The fade-out rule is a threshold on a deterministic model, with an illustrative value. Its threshold was far too low for a population of a few hundred animals; the stochastic version replaces it. - The stochastic model advances in steps of six hours, approximate for the one-day latent period. Bsal arrives as a single infected adult, and the area (20 hectares) sets the population size; results for treatments that let infected animals survive depend on it. - Space is not modelled: the area is one well-mixed population. - Fates are judged within ten years. A population left at a few percent of its former density is counted as remaining. - Treated animals that survive infection never clear it unless `recovery` is on. - The values attached to the switches are illustrative. Different values would change the sizes of the effects, though the contrast between regimes should hold. ## References - Schmidt BR, Bozzuto C, Lötters S, Steinfartz S (2017) Dynamics of host populations affected by the emerging fungal pathogen *Batrachochytrium salamandrivorans*. *Royal Society Open Science* 4:160801.
